questions.title: Why did the D.C. Circuit vacate for lack of standing instead of just affirming the district court's merits dismissal?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the procedural posture here. The district court seems to have reached the merits and concluded that OSC made a legal error about its authority, but still ultimately dismissed AFL's claims. On appeal, the D.C. Circuit says AFL lacked Article III standing and remands with instructions to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. Why does the standing problem require vacating the district court's judgment rather than simply affirming the result? Is this because a federal court that lacks Article III jurisdiction is not allowed to decide the merits at all?

questions.title: How do 5 U.S.C. 7 1216 and FOIA's disciplinary provision in 5 U.S.C. 7 552(a)(4)(F) fit together?
questions.question_body: The opinion discusses two different routes for OSC involvement in alleged FOIA misconduct: section 1216(a)(3), which says OSC 'shall' investigate allegations of arbitrary or capricious FOIA withholding, and FOIA's own provision in section 552(a)(4)(F)(i), which requires OSC to initiate a proceeding only after a court orders production, awards fees, and specifically questions whether the agency acted arbitrarily or capriciously. OSC seems to have treated the FOIA-specific provision as limiting its authority under section 1216, while the district court rejected that view. What is the best way to understand the relationship between these statutes? Does section 552(a)(4)(F) create a mandatory minimum trigger for OSC action, while section 1216 independently authorizes broader investigations, or is there a stronger argument that the more specific FOIA provision should control?

questions.title: Why wasn't AFL's loss of a 'mandatory investigation' enough to count as an Article III injury by itself?
questions.question_body: AFL argued that section 1216 gave it a procedural right to have OSC investigate its allegation, and OSC refused. My instinct was that if Congress says an agency 'shall' do something in response to my complaint, then the agency's failure to do it injures me. But the court says a 'procedural right in vacuo' is not enough and relies on Summers. What exactly is missing here? Is the problem that the procedure was not tied closely enough to a separate concrete interest of AFL's, or that the statute created a duty owed to the public at large rather than to this particular complainant?

questions.title: Why did the court say AFL's FOIA-related injury was not fairly traceable to OSC?
questions.question_body: The court says AFL's inability to get the requested records is traceable to DOJ, not OSC, and that the causal chain through OSC is too speculative. But if OSC had a mandatory duty to investigate arbitrary FOIA withholding, and if that investigation could lead to corrective or disciplinary proceedings, doesn't that at least indirectly affect DOJ's incentives to comply? How do courts decide when an enforcement-related chain of causation becomes too attenuated for standing purposes, especially where the plaintiff is trying to force one agency to police another agency's conduct?

questions.title: Why didn't the relaxed standing rules for procedural injuries help AFL here?
questions.question_body: The opinion says that when a plaintiff alleges violation of a procedural right designed to protect a concrete interest, courts relax imminence and redressability somewhat. But the D.C. Circuit still says AFL fails even under that more forgiving framework. I'm having trouble seeing why. If AFL's concrete interest is access to records or access to investigative information, why isn't an order requiring OSC to perform the allegedly mandatory investigation enough to satisfy the reduced redressability standard? Is the key point that even the relaxed doctrine does not eliminate the need for a non-speculative link between the requested procedure and the concrete benefit?

questions.title: What counts as 'informational standing,' and why didn't AFL qualify for it here?
questions.question_body: The court distinguishes cases like Akins and Public Citizen, where denial of information required by statute was enough for standing, from AFL's claim here. AFL argued that if OSC conducted the investigation, it might receive notices and information associated with section 1214 investigations. The court rejected that because AFL had no statutory entitlement to that information in a section 1216 investigation. Is informational standing always dependent on a clear statutory right to receive specific information, as opposed to a possibility that information may be generated or disclosed during some agency process? If so, how specific does the statute have to be?

questions.title: What exactly was discretionary versus mandatory in OSC's response to an alleged FOIA violation?
questions.question_body: I am struggling with the opinion's treatment of statutory discretion. Section 1216(a)(3) says OSC 'shall' conduct an investigation of any allegation concerning arbitrary or capricious FOIA withholding, which sounds mandatory. But the opinion also emphasizes OSC's enforcement discretion and cites Heckler v. Chaney, and it notes that under Carson the decision whether to use section 1214's notice procedures in a section 1216 investigation is discretionary. So which parts of OSC's conduct are mandatory and which parts remain committed to agency discretion? Is the idea that even if opening some investigation is mandatory, the depth of the investigation, the use of section 1214 procedures, and any follow-on enforcement choices are still discretionary?
